entry.title: Why I Chose Duke’s Online FinTech Master’s While Working Full Time | Wyatt Williams

media:group.media:title: Why I Chose Duke’s Online FinTech Master’s While Working Full Time | Wyatt Williams
media:group.media:description:
Meet Wyatt Williams, a fintech solutions engineer earning his Duke Master of Engineering in FinTech online while working full time and raising a family.
After nearly a decade working with banks and credit unions across North America, Wyatt saw a gap in his technical skills and decided to close it. In this video he explains why he chose Duke's FinTech program, what hands-on learning looks like from the first semester, how his team built a real-time digital asset portfolio analysis tool, and how he balances graduate school with work and family.
CHAPTERS 0:00 Meet Wyatt Williams 0:20 Closing a technical skills gap in a fintech career 0:44 Why Wyatt chose Duke's FinTech program 1:19 Industry connections and the online cohort 1:48 Applied, hands-on learning from the first semester 2:19 Building a digital asset portfolio analysis tool with live APIs 3:29 A day in the life of a working professional in grad school 4:01 Family support and what keeps Wyatt going
QUICK ANSWERS
What is the Duke Master of Engineering in FinTech? It is a Master of Engineering program at Duke's Pratt School of Engineering built around fintech and connected directly to the industry. Wyatt chose it for the exposure to professionals who have worked at major banks, fintechs, and in mortgage, and for the direct access students have to them.
Can you earn Duke's FinTech master's online? Yes. Wyatt is part of the online cohort. He describes professors who include online students in the on-campus classroom experience so they feel part of the same program.
Is the program hands-on or theoretical? Wyatt describes it as very applied. Students write code and build things from the first semester, and the program builds on those skills with team projects in the following semester.
What do students build in the FinTech program? In his software engineering course, Wyatt's online cohort built a real-time portfolio analysis tool for digital assets such as cryptocurrencies. A market data company provided student API access, so the tool ran on live data. Team members took roles such as lead engineer, product manager, and UI expert.
How do you balance a full-time job, family, and grad school? Wyatt uses his mornings and evenings. Before his family is up, he reviews lecture notes, watches lectures at his own pace, and works on homework. He credits his wife and daughter for their support.

entry.title: Meet Diya Mirji | MEng AI for Product Innovation | From Software Engineer to AI for Women’s Health

media:group.media:title: Meet Diya Mirji | MEng AI for Product Innovation | From Software Engineer to AI for Women’s Health
media:group.media:description:
Meet Diya Mirji, a Duke Pratt Master of Engineering student in AI for Product Innovation (AIPI), working on AI trust and safety and elephant conservation.
Diya started her career as a software engineer specializing in intelligent systems. She came to Duke to learn how to use data responsibly and to apply AI to real problems, not just study theory. In this video she explains why she chose the AIPI program, what she is building in research, and why she wants a career in AI for women's health.
CHAPTERS 0:00 Meet Diya Mirji 0:13 From software engineer to AI for Product Innovation 0:39 Why Diya chose Duke's AIPI program 0:52 Research projects: the Trust Lab and AI trust and safety 1:10 Using machine learning to identify elephants in Thailand 2:12 The capstone: three months working with a real company 2:43 What it means to study in person at Duke 2:54 AIPI Ladies Night and building confidence 4:03 Career goals: AI for women's health 4:26 Why women's health needs better answers
QUICK ANSWERS
What is the AI for Product Innovation program at Duke? AIPI is a Master of Engineering program at Duke's Pratt School of Engineering. Students apply AI knowledge in practice, including a capstone where teams work with a real company for three months on a problem the company needs solved.
What research do AIPI students do? Diya works on three projects. Two are with the Trust Lab, which focuses on improving trust and safety in AI. The third is an elephant conservation project with Duke's Nicholas School of the Environment.
How can machine learning help protect elephants and farmers? Using camera trap images from Thailand, Diya's team is building a model that uniquely identifies individual elephants and classifies whether male elephants have tusks. Tusked males are considered more aggressive, so identifying them could help alert authorities and reduce risk of injury to both elephants and farmers.
What is AIPI Ladies Night? A gathering for women in the AIPI program to connect and talk about anything, including confidence and making sure their ideas and experience are heard.
Why does Diya want to work in AI for women's health? She wants to build technology that improves care and gives patients more specific answers than "stress" or "hormones."

entry.title: How Duke Helps Engineers Go From Lab to Startup (Step by Step) | Pratt Blueprint Episode 3

media:group.media:title: How Duke Helps Engineers Go From Lab to Startup (Step by Step) | Pratt Blueprint Episode 3
media:group.media:description:
Engineers who want to start a company need more than a great technology. In this episode of The Blueprint, Duke founders Cambre Kelly and David Smith share their journeys from research to company, and Vinik Dean of Engineering Jerry Lynch sits down with Ibrahim Mohedas, Executive in Residence at Pratt, to explore the programs that help students and faculty become founders.
Questions this video answers
Why is a PhD an advantage for becoming a founder? Cambre Kelly says a PhD combines deep technical skill with professional training in problem solving, and a startup needs both to solve technical problems and business problems like fundraising and team organization.
How does Duke research become a company? Restor3D, founded in 2017, is a Duke spinout based on research from Ken Gall's lab in Mechanical Engineering and Materials Science. The company uses preoperative CT scans to design implants for individual patients.
What does Duke offer to help turn research into a company? Kelly and David Smith describe support from Duke's Office of Translation and Commercialization, which helps with licensing agreements and patent prosecution, and from Duke Capital Partners, which has participated in financing rounds. Smith says Duke's flexibility on deal terms helped his metamaterials research reach the market.
What is the PhD Startup Accelerator? Ibrahim Mohedas says the Christensen Family Center for Innovation accelerator introduces faculty and PhD students to customer discovery, value proposition thinking, and building a pitch that is startup oriented instead of research oriented.
What is the customer discovery program? Mohedas trains undergraduates to run customer discovery research for PhD students and faculty. He says students can complete 50 to 100 interviews in a semester, where a PhD student might complete one or two. Lumius Imaging was accepted to Y Combinator on its second try after adding that data to its application.
Where can Duke startups find lab and office space? The BRiDGE Incubator, in the Chesterfield Building downtown, gives early-stage startups office space, wet lab space, and shared equipment when funds are tight. Mohedas also describes the Duke Founders Network, a community where founders learn from each other.

entry.title: Hidden in the Walls: Developing Technologies to Combat Mold in Coastal NC | I/O Digital Feature

media:group.media:title: Hidden in the Walls: Developing Technologies to Combat Mold in Coastal NC | I/O Digital Feature
media:group.media:description:
For residents of coastal North Carolina, concerns about mold permeate everyday life. Community members are looking for answers, and Duke researchers are collaborating with them to develop solutions they can trust.
At the NSF Engineering Research Center for Precision Microbiome Engineering (PreMiEr), researchers from Duke, UNC and NC State are working together to study how the microbes in our everyday living environments impact human health. Interviews with residents in 22 households in Carteret County, North Carolina integrate community experiences and priorities into the center’s mold research, including the need for affordable solutions and transparency around newly introduced technologies.
Armed with this knowledge, the PreMiER team is developing sensors that detect chemical compounds released by mold, with the goal of using robotics and artificial intelligence to help locate problems that may be hidden behind walls. Ultimately, the researchers hope to bring mold detection from the lab into homes at a lower cost, supporting earlier detection, more targeted remediation, and healthier living spaces.
Learn more about PreMiEr: https://premier-microbiome.org/ Learn more about Duke Engineering: https://pratt.duke.edu/

entry.title: The Pocket Colposcope: Bringing Cervical Cancer Screening to Women Worldwide | I/O Digital Feature

media:group.media:title: The Pocket Colposcope: Bringing Cervical Cancer Screening to Women Worldwide | I/O Digital Feature
media:group.media:description:
The Pocket Colposcope is a low-cost, portable device that brings cervical cancer screening to women in places where traditional equipment is out of reach.
Developed by Nimmi Ramanujam, the Robert W. Carr Professor of Biomedical Engineering at Duke University and partners at the Duke School of Medicine, the technology pairs portable imaging with artificial intelligence and digital health tools. It supports earlier detection, consistent quality control, and screening in low-resource and rural settings.
Ramanujam founded Duke's Global Women's Health Technologies program in 2013 and launched Calla Health in 2019 to bring the Pocket Colposcope to patients. The device has reached more than 8,000 women across 11 countries. In 2026, she was elected to the National Academy of Engineering.
Read the full story: https://pratt.duke.edu/news/ramanujam-nae-2026/ Explore Global Women's Health Technologies: https://www.dukegwht.org/ Learn more about Duke Engineering: https://pratt.duke.edu/

entry.title: How Engineers and Doctors Are Transforming Health Care | Pratt Blueprint Episode 2

media:group.media:title: How Engineers and Doctors Are Transforming Health Care | Pratt Blueprint Episode 2
media:group.media:description:
How do engineers work with nurses, clinicians and medical doctors to solve some of the most difficult problems facing medicine and healthcare today? The health issues around the globe that countless people experience cannot be solved by medical experts alone. According to the American Cancer Society, by 2050, cancer cases are predicted to increase to 35 million people based on projected population growth. In 2022, 9.7 million people died from the disease worldwide. For diabetes cases, according to the World Health Organization, over 830 million people are living with diabetes in 2022. So what can we do as a society to help prevent or "find, track, and treat" these health issues through interdisciplinary work being done on Duke's campus, where engineers and clinicians work side by side to improve health outcomes and prevent issues before they arise?
Hear from four experts in environmental engineering, biomedical engineering, and mechanical engineering on the advances in science and engineering happening today. Jerome P. Lynch, Vinik Dean of Engineering at the Pratt School of Engineering, hosts and narrates.
In this episode: Claudia Gunsch is an environmental engineer who directs PreMiEr, Duke's NSF Engineering Research Center for Precision Microbiome Engineering (PreMiEr). Her team studies the bacteria and fungi in buildings and designs sensors to detect harmful pathogens before they reach a patient. (https://premier-microbiome.org/)
Digital twins are Amanda Randles' focus as director of the Duke Center for Computational and Digital Health Innovation. Her lab builds patient-specific models from CT scans, MRIs, and wearable data, updated continuously to track a person's health in real time. (https://comphealth.duke.edu/)
Joanna Bertram, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering and materials science, designs steerable needles and continuum robots for minimally invasive surgery, reaching biopsy sites without a large incision. (https://mems.duke.edu/people/joanna-bertram/)
Neural engineering brings together Cameron McIntyre's work in biomedical engineering and neurosurgery. His lab combines MRI and brain mapping to guide treatments like deep brain stimulation and focused ultrasound, including Duke's recent use of focused ultrasound for tremor. (https://bme.duke.edu/people/cameron-mcintyre/)
We explore how engineering and medicine can work together to advance disease prevention, early detection, personalized care, minimally invasive surgery, and treatments for neurological conditions.
Featured topics include: precision microbiome engineering, healthy buildings, pathogen detection, digital twins in healthcare, wearable health data, surgical robotics, neural engineering, deep brain stimulation, and focused ultrasound.
